name: Yoel Romero
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1999 World Wrestling Championships gold medal at 85 kg freestyle at age 22, followed by Olympic silver at the 2000 Sydney Games at age 23.
early_history_summary: Romero was scouted by Cuban state sports coaches at age eight based on physical attributes and channeled into a specialist wrestling school. He came from a fighting family—his father was on the Cuban national boxing team and his half-brother Yoan Pablo Hernandez became a world boxing champion. Romero placed fifth at the 1997 Senior World Championships at age 20, won bronze in 1998, and became world champion in 1999 by defeating 1996 Olympic gold medalist Khadzhimurad Magomedov.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and state scouting system
family_context_summary: Born in Pinar del Río, Cuba; father was on the Cuban national boxing team and half-brother Yoan Pablo Hernandez was a professional world boxing champion. Family deeply embedded in Cuban combat sports culture.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a member of the Cuban national boxing team; half-brother became a world boxing champion. Combat sports were a family domain, though Yoel was directed into wrestling rather than boxing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Cuban state sports system, early scouting, family combat sports, physical prodigy
evidence_summary: Romero was scouted at age eight by Cuban state coaches and placed in a specialist wrestling school, reflecting the country's systematic talent identification pipeline. His father boxed for the Cuban national team and his half-brother became a world boxing champion, giving him a family-domain advantage in combat sports. By age 20 he was competing at senior World Championship level, winning gold at 22 and Olympic silver at 23. The Cuban sports system provided elite coaching, facilities, and international competition access from a young age.
starting_point: Born in Pinar del Río, Cuba to a family embedded in combat sports; father was on the Cuban national boxing team and half-brother became a world boxing champion.
current_position: Still active in combat sports at age 48, competing in BKFC and bareknuckle MMA events; resides in Miami, Florida.

trajectory.event: Placed fifth at the Senior World Wrestling Championships in his international debut.
Won gold at the World Wrestling Championships at 85 kg, defeating 1996 Olympic gold medalist Magomedov.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Sydney Olympics in freestyle wrestling at 85 kg.
Won gold at the Pan American Games in Santo Domingo at 84 kg freestyle.
Made UFC debut after transitioning to MMA, quickly becoming a top middleweight contender.
Signed with BKFC and continued competing in bareknuckle MMA events, defying age expectations.

name: Claude Nicollier
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Nicollier graduated with a BSc in physics in 1970 (age 26) and qualified as a Swiss Air Force pilot in 1966, but his astronaut selection came in 1978 (age 34) and first spaceflight in 1992 (age 48).
early_history_summary: Nicollier graduated from the Gymnase de Lausanne in 1962, earned a BSc in physics from the University of Lausanne in 1970, and qualified as a Swiss Air Force pilot in 1966. He later earned an MSc in astrophysics from the University of Geneva in 1975 and became a Swissair DC-9 pilot in 1974.
evidence_summary: Nicollier's path to space was long: he earned his physics degree at 26, his master's in astrophysics at 31, and was selected as an ESA astronaut at 34. His first spaceflight did not occur until 1992 when he was 48. No material, independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Annie Lennox
milestone_by_age_26: As vocalist of The Tourists, reached #4 on the UK Singles Chart with 'I Only Want to Be with You' in November 1979 at age 24, followed by a second top-10 hit in early 1980.
early_history_summary: Born in a working-class Aberdeen neighborhood, Lennox showed musical talent early—playing piano at age three, joining a choir at six, and learning flute at eleven. At seventeen she won a scholarship to London's Royal Academy of Music but left before completing her degree. She met guitarist Dave Stewart in the mid-1970s while working at a London restaurant, and they formed The Tourists, releasing three albums between 1979 and 1980.
family_context_summary: Born to Dorothy Farquharson and Thomas Allison Lennox in a working-class neighborhood in Aberdeen, Scotland. Mother was a cook, father was a welder in a local shipyard. Family was not wealthy but supported her musical education.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental music profession; father was a welder and mother a cook. Parents noticed and supported her early musical talent with piano lessons from age seven.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dave Stewart partnership, Royal Academy scholarship, working-class drive, new wave wave
evidence_summary: Lennox grew up in a working-class Aberdeen household with a welder father and cook mother, but showed early musical talent that earned her a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Music at 17. She left before graduating and spent several years working day jobs while singing at night. Her pivotal break came when she met Dave Stewart, forming The Tourists, which produced a #4 UK hit in 1979 when she was 24. The Stewart-Lennox creative partnership became the foundation for Eurythmics and her subsequent solo career.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Aberdeen, Scotland; father was a shipyard welder and mother a cook, who supported her early musical interests with piano lessons.
current_position: Living in retirement from active recording; OBE recipient and political activist focused on humanitarian causes; resides in the UK.

trajectory.event: Reached #4 on the UK Singles Chart with The Tourists' 'I Only Want to Be with You,' establishing her as a charting artist.
Formed Eurythmics with Dave Stewart and released their debut album In the Garden.
Eurythmics' 'Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)' hit #1 on the US Billboard Hot 100, achieving global stardom.
Released solo debut album Diva, which sold over 2 million copies and earned multiple Grammy nominations.
Inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Eurythmics.

name: Revaz Gabriadze
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Gabriadze debuted as a screenwriter in 1968 at age 32 and founded his puppet theatre in 1981 at age 45; no independently verifiable creative milestone occurred by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Kutaisi, Georgia, Gabriadze graduated from the Higher Scriptwriters' Courses in Moscow and worked as a correspondent for the newspaper Youth of Georgia before entering cinema. His first screenwriting credit came in 1968 with the film An Unusual Exhibition.
evidence_summary: Gabriadze's first documented creative work was his 1968 screenwriting debut at age 32. His major achievements—co-writing Mimino (1977) and Kin-dza-dza! (1986), and founding the Marionette Theatre (1981)—all came well after age 26. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Marco Pantani
milestone_by_age_26: Finished second overall at the 1994 Giro d'Italia with two stage wins, and placed third overall at the 1994 Tour de France, both at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Cesena to a working-class family—his father Paolo was an engineer and his mother Tonina a chambermaid—Pantani joined the Fausto Coppi cycling club of Cesenatico at age eleven. As an amateur he won the 1992 Girobio (amateur Giro d'Italia) after finishing third in 1990 and second in 1991, then turned professional later that year. In 1994, his second Grand Tour, he won two mountain stages at the Giro d'Italia and finished second overall, then took third at the Tour de France.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class family in Cesenatico; father was an engineer and mother a chambermaid. His grandfather bought him his first bike and a neighbor suggested he join the local cycling club.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental cycling background; father was an engineer, mother a chambermaid. Family supported his cycling but had no domain expertise in the sport.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Fausto Coppi cycling club, early cycling start, climbing talent, amateur Girobio win
evidence_summary: Pantani grew up in a working-class family in Cesenatico and joined the local Fausto Coppi cycling club at age eleven after a neighbor's suggestion. He showed exceptional climbing ability from the start, progressing through amateur categories with Girobio finishes of 3rd, 2nd, and 1st (1990-1992). After turning professional in 1992, he burst onto the Grand Tour scene in 1994 with a second-place Giro d'Italia finish and two stage wins, followed by third overall at the Tour de France—all at age 24. His climbing talent was the primary engine, honed by years of repetition in the hills of Emilia-Romagna.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Cesena/Cesenatico, Italy; father was an engineer, mother a chambermaid, with no cycling background in the family.
current_position: Died on February 14, 2004 at age 34 in Rimini, Italy; final role: professional cyclist, 1998 Giro d'Italia and Tour de France winner.

trajectory.event: Won the Girobio (amateur Giro d'Italia) and turned professional with Carrera Jeans–Vagabond.
Finished second overall at the Giro d'Italia with two stage wins and third overall at the Tour de France, establishing himself as a Grand Tour contender.
Won both the Giro d'Italia and the Tour de France, becoming one of only eight riders to achieve the double.
Expelled from the Giro d'Italia while leading by over five minutes due to irregular blood values, marking the beginning of his decline.
Found dead in a Rimini hotel room from an accidental cocaine overdose after years of depression and near-inactivity.

name: Kunishige Kamamoto
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic bronze medal with Japan at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, finishing as the tournament's top scorer with seven goals, at age 24.
early_history_summary: Born in Kyoto, Kamamoto attended Yamashiro High School before joining Waseda University's School of Commerce. He was the top scorer in the Kanto university league for four consecutive years and won the Emperor's Cup in 1963 and 1966 with Waseda—the last time a university team won that competition. He competed at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 20, then joined Yanmar Diesel in 1967 before his breakout 1968 Olympics.
family_context_summary: Born in Kyoto, Japan; family background not documented in reviewed sources beyond his place of birth and education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Waseda University, Emperor's Cup, Tokyo Olympics, national team pipeline
evidence_summary: Kamamoto attended Waseda University, where he was the top scorer in the Kanto university league for four straight years and won the Emperor's Cup twice—achievements that placed him in Japan's national team pipeline. He competed at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics at age 20 and won bronze at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics as tournament top scorer with seven goals at age 24. The Waseda University football program and national team selection by coach Dettmar Cramer were key institutional accelerants. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Kyoto, Japan; family background not documented, but attended Waseda University, an elite institution, suggesting at least middle-class educational access.
current_position: Died on August 10, 2025 at age 81 in Osaka, Japan; final roles: Japan's all-time leading goalscorer (75 goals in 76 matches), former House of Councillors member, JFA vice president.

trajectory.event: Competed at the Tokyo Olympics, scoring his first Olympic goal in a loss to Yugoslavia.
Won the Emperor's Cup with Waseda University, the last university team to achieve this feat.
Won Olympic bronze at Mexico City and finished as tournament top scorer with seven goals, including two against France and two against Mexico.
Led Yanmar Diesel to their first Japan Soccer League championship as top scorer.
Became player-manager of Yanmar Diesel, later leading the club to the 1980 league title.
Elected to Japan's House of Councillors, serving as a national legislator until 2001.
Inducted into the Japan Football Hall of Fame.
Died of pneumonia in Osaka Prefecture on August 10, 2025.

name: Željko Franulović
milestone_by_age_26: Reached the 1970 French Open final and won the Monte-Carlo Masters in the same year, at age 23, reaching a career-high world ranking of No. 8 in March 1971.
early_history_summary: Born on the island of Korčula and raised in Split, Franulović learned tennis at a sport club in Split that also produced Nikola Pilić. He played his first singles tournament at the 1963 Yugoslavian International Championships at age 16 and won his first title at the same event in 1967 at age 20. His breakthrough came in 1970 with the French Open final and Monte Carlo title.
primary_leverage_engine: Early tennis specialization in a regional tennis center
family_context_summary: Born on the island of Korčula to father Ivo and mother Katica; moved to Split at one month old. Family background beyond this is not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. He learned tennis at a sport club in Split, one of Yugoslavia's main tennis centers, but no family tennis background is documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Split tennis club, Yugoslav tennis center, early tournament play, French Open final
evidence_summary: Franulović grew up in Split, one of Yugoslavia's main tennis centers, and learned the sport at a local club that also produced Nikola Pilić. He began competing at 16 and won his first title at 20. His 1970 season—reaching the French Open final and winning Monte Carlo—established him among the world's top players at age 23. The Split tennis ecosystem provided early facilities and peer competition, though family financial or tennis background is not documented.
starting_point: Born on the island of Korčula, Yugoslavia (now Croatia) to father Ivo and mother Katica; moved to Split as an infant where he grew up and learned tennis at a local sport club.
current_position: Serving as Monte-Carlo Masters tournament director since 2005; resides in Monaco region; age 78.

trajectory.event: Won his first professional singles title at the Yugoslavian International Championships.
Reached the French Open final (lost to Jan Kodeš) and won the Monte-Carlo Masters, establishing himself as a top-tier player.
Reached a career-high world ranking of No. 8 in March and the French Open semifinals.
Won the Munich singles title, one of 23 career singles titles.
Became tournament director of the Monte-Carlo Masters, a role he has held for two decades.

name: Alexey Ekimov
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Ekimov graduated from St. Petersburg University in 1967 (age ~22) and earned his PhD in 1974 (age ~29). His discovery of quantum dots came in 1981 (age ~36), and the Nobel Prize in 2023 (age ~78).
early_history_summary: Ekimov studied at the Department of Solid State Physics at St. Petersburg University, graduating in 1967. He then worked at the Ioffe Institute and the Vavilov State Optical Institute, earning his PhD in 1974 with a dissertation on optical orientation of carrier spins in semiconductors. His groundbreaking quantum dots research began in the early 1980s.
evidence_summary: Ekimov was a brilliant student at St. Petersburg University, graduating in 1967, but his material scientific achievements came later: his PhD in 1974, the State Prize in 1976, and the discovery of quantum dots in 1981. No independently verifiable material milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Krisztina Egerszegi
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold in the 200m backstroke at the 1988 Seoul Olympics at age 14, becoming the youngest-ever female Olympic swimming champion, and added a silver in the 100m backstroke.
early_history_summary: Born in Budapest, Egerszegi began swimming at age four under Miklós Kiss. She was identified as talented early and sent to coach György Turi at age six, then to Hungarian national team coach László Kiss at age twelve. She made her international debut at the 1987 European Championships at age 13, placing fourth in the 200m backstroke. At the 1988 Olympics, weighing only 46 kg, she won gold in the 200m backstroke and silver in the 100m backstroke at age 14.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and early coaching pipeline
family_context_summary: Born in Budapest, Hungary; family background not documented in detail in reviewed sources. She began swimming at age four and was channeled into the Hungarian swimming pipeline through early coaching identification.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Her early swimming was initiated through a children's swim program, not through family swimming background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: László Kiss coaching, Budapesti Spartacus SC, Hungarian swimming pipeline, prodigy, early Olympic debut
evidence_summary: Egerszegi started swimming at age four in Budapest and was quickly identified as talented, moving through a structured coaching pipeline: Miklós Kiss (age 4-5), György Turi (age 6-12), and then László Kiss, the Hungarian national team coach, from age 12. This sustained, high-quality individualized coaching from an early age was the key accelerant. At 14, she won Olympic gold in the 200m backstroke at Seoul, becoming the youngest female Olympic swimming champion ever. Her ideal backstroke physique and natural ability were recognized and refined by her coaches from the start.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungary; family background not documented in detail, but she began swimming at age four and was channeled into the Hungarian national swimming pipeline through early coaching identification.
current_position: Living a private life in Érd, Hungary; serves as ambassador for the Úszó Nemzet (Swimming Nation) Program promoting children's swimming; retired from competitive swimming at age 22 in 1996.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic gold in the 200m backstroke and silver in the 100m backstroke at the Seoul Olympics, becoming the youngest-ever female Olympic swimming champion.
Won double gold in both backstroke events at the World Championships in Perth.
Won three individual Olympic gold medals at Barcelona (100m backstroke, 200m backstroke, 400m IM), becoming the only female swimmer to win three individual events at one Olympics.
Won her third consecutive Olympic gold in the 200m backstroke at Atlanta, then retired from competitive swimming.
Inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame.
Became ambassador for the Úszó Nemzet Program, promoting water safety and swimming for Hungarian children.

name: Peter O'Leary
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. O'Leary began refereeing in 1994 at age 22, but did not receive his FIFA referee badge until 2003 (age 31) and officiated at his first World Cup in 2010 (age 38).
early_history_summary: Born in Wellington, New Zealand, O'Leary switched from playing to refereeing at age 21 in 1994. He officiated in the New Zealand Football Championship and later the Australian A-League, but his international career began only when he became FIFA-listed in 2003.
evidence_summary: O'Leary began refereeing at 22 but achieved no material milestone by age 26. His FIFA listing came at 31, his first World Cup at 38, and his career peak was officiating at the 2010 and 2014 FIFA World Cups. No independently verifiable milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Khalifa Haftar
milestone_by_age_26: No material independently verifiable personal milestone by age 26 found. Haftar graduated from the Royal Military Academy in 1966 (age ~23) and participated in the 1969 coup as a junior officer implementing others' plans, but his significant military command roles came in the 1980s and his political leadership in the 2010s.
early_history_summary: Born in Ajdabiya, Libya, Haftar received secondary education in Derna before enrolling in the Benghazi Royal Military Academy in 1964, graduating as an artillery officer in 1966. He was a member of the Free Officers movement that helped Gaddafi overthrow the monarchy in 1969, but was not part of the core Revolutionary Command Council.
family_context_summary: Born in Ajdabiya, Libya; member of the Firjan tribe, a medium-size clan. Father's profession not clearly documented; one source describes him as the son of a Libyan military officer.
parent_family_domain_summary: One source mentions his father was a Libyan military officer, but this is not independently confirmed across multiple sources.
evidence_summary: Haftar graduated from the Royal Military Academy at ~23 and was a junior participant in the 1969 coup that brought Gaddafi to power, but his role was limited to implementing plans made by Gaddafi's inner circle. His significant military commands—leading forces in Chad in the 1980s and commanding the Libyan National Army in the 2010s—came decades later. No material personal milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Wladimir Resnitschenko
milestone_by_age_26: Won team épée gold at the 1987 World Championships representing the Soviet Union at age 22, followed by Olympic team épée bronze at the 1988 Seoul Olympics at age 23.
early_history_summary: Born to a Russian mother and Cuban father in Almaty, Kazakhstan, Resnitschenko lived in Tallinn, Estonia from 1984 and was trained as a fencing coach there from 1985 to 1989. He competed for Dynamo Tallinn and the Soviet national team, winning the World Championship team gold in 1987 and Olympic team bronze in 1988. He later defected to West Germany in 1990 and won Olympic team gold for Germany in 1992.
primary_leverage_engine: Soviet fencing pipeline and tactical skill
family_context_summary: Born to a Russian mother and Cuban father in Almaty, Kazakhstan (then Soviet Union). His father studied in Moscow. Family background beyond this is not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of family fencing background; father was Cuban and studied in Moscow. The Soviet sports system, not family, appears to have been the primary pathway into fencing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet fencing system, Dynamo Tallinn, World Championship gold, left-handed tactical advantage
evidence_summary: Resnitschenko was born in Almaty to a Russian mother and Cuban father and entered the Soviet fencing pipeline, training at Dynamo Tallinn from 1984. The Soviet sports system provided elite coaching, facilities, and competition access. By 22, he was World Championship team gold medalist, and at 23 he won Olympic team bronze. His left-handedness and tactical acumen were noted advantages. Family fencing background is not documented; the Soviet institutional pipeline was the primary accelerant.
starting_point: Born to a Russian mother and Cuban father in Almaty, Kazakh SSR, Soviet Union; father studied in Moscow; family moved through the Soviet sports system.
current_position: Working as a fencing coach in Germany after returning from a coaching stint in Russia; resides in Germany.

trajectory.event: Won team épée gold at the World Championships representing the Soviet Union, finishing fifth individually.
Won Olympic team épée bronze at the Seoul Olympics representing the Soviet Union; finished eighth individually.
Defected to West Germany during a World Cup meeting in Italy, seeking new citizenship and opportunities.
Won Olympic team épée gold at the Barcelona Olympics representing Germany and won the German national title.
Received the Silver Bay Leaf, Germany's highest sports award, and turned to coaching, initially moving to Russia.
